crypto-lab-collision-vault.note: The lab hashes with WebCrypto through one local helper, and names the algorithm only as that helper's STRING ARGUMENT: hashing/index.ts:79 is `return webcryptoDigest('SHA-256', bytes)` and :81 the SHA-512 case, while webcrypto.ts:25 does the work as `subtle().digest(algo, copy)` with algo a parameter. No line carries both the name and the operation, so no detection shape can reach it, and the only other place either name appears in executable code is a vectors table (SHA256_VECTORS, SHA512_VECTORS) - which is test data, not an implementation, and is now correctly suppressed. Reviewed by reading hashing/index.ts and hashing/webcrypto.ts in full: both digests are computed by the platform on the learner's input, which is the lab's whole subject. Anchored at the call sites rather than at the digest call, because those are the lines that say WHICH algorithm.

crypto-lab-function-key.note: Browser TypeScript throughout, no other language and no WASM. Group operations are @noble/curves 2.4.0, pinned to RFC 9496 Appendix A (16 A.1 multiples both directions, 29 A.2 rejections, 8 A.3 map outputs) before any scheme code was written on it; ABDP15 Construction 3.1 and the baby-step giant-step, exact-rational and mod-l algebra are implemented in-repo. Five derived attacks are removed because none is an attack this lab shows, and each was matched by a different accident: Man-in-the-middle came from the string 'DH MITM' inside CATALOG-ENTRY.md, which is this catalog's own concept line quoted back in the lab's handoff doc and not lab source at all; Signature malleability from /malleab/i on a seed label, in a lab that has no signatures - what it demonstrates is CIPHERTEXT malleability, and its own source calls that 'not an attack and not a flaw in the proof'; Chosen-plaintext attack from CPA inside 'IND-FE-CPA', the security notion ABDP15 proves rather than an attack mounted; Chosen-ciphertext attack from CCA inside 'Any CCA security whatever', a line in the NOT-BUILT list; and Discrete log from 'baby step', which this lab pays as a decryption cost and never mounts. The two attacks it does show, key collusion and ciphertext malleability, have no term in the vocabulary. Baby-step giant-step is added by review: src/crypto/dlog.ts is a baby-step giant-step over a symmetric range, but it names the algorithm only in comments and in the local counters babySteps and giantSteps, and the exported function is called dlogSymmetric. The anchor is that function, not the counter a narrower shape used to read. Re-reviewed at b145a348de0771eed22923c1da210c60e961bbf6 on 2026-10-09: compared the prior pin to current source; the only implementation change preserves disclosures and focused summaries during worker-driven redraws in src/main.ts. Read the current README, IPFE setup/key derivation/encryption/decryption and symmetric bounded BSGS. The cryptographic implementation, selective IND-FE-CPA/DDH scope, no-integrity limitation, reviewed additions and five exclusions remain unchanged. Current lab tests and deployed resource identity are recorded separately in the fleet evidence.

The browser performs real Ed25519 verification with extended-coordinate BigInt arithmetic and WebCrypto SHA-512; both modes share decoder, challenge and equation, and differ only on S < L enforcement. The Ed25519 anchor is its verifier entry rather than the UI import. The Python file only cross-checks frozen fixtures with OpenSSL and libsodium; it is not hidden browser crypto. RE-READ 2026-10-04 after this lab was re-framed to lead with the forgery (crypto-lab-vector-gate#7). src/crypto/ed25519.ts and tools/check-oracles.py are BYTE-IDENTICAL to the previously reviewed commit, and both anchors still resolve to what this note describes -- line 74 is the verifier entry, line 85 the WebCrypto SHA-512 digest. The two claims above that are about main.ts were re-checked rather than assumed: side-channel resistance is still mentioned only as evidence NOT established, and ZIP215 and ML-KEM still appear only as prose pointing at other labs, with no computation of either here. crypto-lab-locks-and-keys.note: Read src/crypto/pair.ts, lock.ts, sign.ts, vectors.ts, pinned.ts and vectors.test.ts. One 2048-bit RSA pair does two different jobs: RSAES-OAEP encryption and RSASSA-PSS signing. The page is careful that signing is NOT encryption run backwards, and the scanner's RSA / RSA-OAEP / RSA-PSS / SHA-256 anchors are the real WebCrypto call sites. Two negative claims are carried in the lab rather than implied: a successful decryption establishes nothing about WHO encrypted the message, since anyone holding the public half could have; and a verifying signature ties a note to a KEY, not to a person. Correctness rests on 12 pinned Project Wycheproof cases -- 6 OAEP and 6 PSS, of which 4 must be REFUSED -- taken from rsa_oaep_2048_sha256_mgf1sha256_test.json and rsa_pss_2048_sha256_mgf1_32_test.json and run in the reader's own browser. RFC 8017 is cited for the SCHEMES only (§7.1 RSAES-OAEP, §8.1 RSASSA-PSS) and never for the numbers, because RFC 8017 publishes no test data; src/crypto/vectors.test.ts asserts that attribution cannot drift. The build brief's claim of 'a pinned RSA-OAEP / RSA-PSS vector from RFC 8017's test data' was wrong and is corrected in audits/BRIEF-locks-and-keys.md.

The scanner anchored both at line 1, which is the IMPORT line in each file; the pins above move them to the operations, so the index points at work rather than at a dependency. The remove list below now does what the sentence claimed. The lab's own argument is that ML-KEM is not STRONGER than X25519 but rests on a different hard problem, with the measurable difference being size on the wire.

crypto-lab-https-padlock.note: Read src/pki/path.ts, parse.ts, assess.ts, break.ts and src/tls/clienthello.ts. The scanner found only X25519 in the ClientHello builder. The chain walk really does verify every signature: src/pki/path.ts:86 calls @peculiar/x509's verify with the parent's public key and the WebCrypto provider, over real DER TBS bytes, and the certificates this lab ships are ECDSA over P-256 and P-384 -- so ECDSA is pinned above. Scope that the card and chips are written to respect: the lab makes NO network connection and runs no handshake, so it never observes encryption; it reads certificates captured earlier. Its RFC 5280 path validation is a stated teaching subset, deliberately omitting revocation, name constraints, policy constraints and path length, so a chain this page accepts is not thereby a chain a browser would accept. The ClientHello is encoded byte for byte and never sent, and its X25519 private half is discarded unused -- which is why the chip is marked 'ClientHello Bytes Only' rather than claiming TLS 1.3. Trust terminates in the lab's own committed copy of a root list, not the reader's device trust store, and the page says so.

crypto-lab-good-randomness.note: Read src/crypto/chacha20.ts, cipher.ts, pinned.ts and vectors.ts. ChaCha20 is HAND-ROLLED here rather than imported, because it is the teaching subject and a reader has to be able to open the file: the scanner anchored it at src/crypto/pinned.ts:18, which is that file's import line, so the pin moves it to the block function it actually implements. AES-GCM and SHA-256 come from crypto.subtle and their anchors are the real call sites. The lab's point is that a generator seeded from a guessable value produces guessable keys while every check on the page still reports success -- the key from a four-digit PIN is rebuilt by trying ten thousand seeds, which is counting rather than cryptanalysis.
